text: A real peer review doesn't say 'looks good' and move on -- it reads the actual logic and names the path nobody tested. Lesson 17's test plan already proved this discipline works, finding a real Prairie View defect through an edge case, not the clean demo path. This lesson runs that same discipline one layer up, against a part of the build no test case has touched: the Access-request approval subflow Lesson 15 built.

A reviewing architect reads that subflow and raises a specific finding: it fails closed correctly when a requester's manager sits in the wrong domain, refusing to guess at an approver. But a null return from that check just stops the subflow. If a cross-domain mismatch ever happens in production, an employee's legitimate access request silently never gets approved -- no error reaches them, no one in their domain is notified, the ticket simply sits there.

The reviewer isn't arguing the original decision was wrong. Refusing to auto-approve across a domain boundary that was never supposed to be crossed is exactly correct, and reversing it would reintroduce the real risk the subflow exists to prevent. The gap is treating that refusal as a complete answer when it's only half of one -- and the fix doesn't need new machinery. Lesson 15's own routing script already falls back to a named, documented queue instead of guessing or dropping a request silently.

The revision gives the approval subflow that same shape of answer. When the approver check returns null, the request routes to a domain's defined escalation group instead of stopping, and the requester gets notified their request needs manual review rather than watching it disappear. The domain boundary is never crossed by auto-approving -- a real person in the right place gets the chance to resolve it, instead of the request vanishing from view.

A safe failure nobody can see is still a failure an employee experiences as 'the new system lost my request' -- exactly the kind of silent breakage that would undercut the trust Lesson 13's Prairie View interview spent a whole lesson establishing. Taking a specific critique like this seriously, and revising in response, is a stronger signal in an interview than a build nobody ever challenged. Next, this finished, now-revised capstone gets packaged into the portfolio piece Chapter 3 described how to write.
